candidateRows: Christian commitments make salvation and relationship with Christ universally available through many dimensions of ordinary human life.
This establishes the Catholic premise against which hiddenness must be assessed while proposing socially mediated access rather than access restricted to intellectual elites.
O'Connor's framing of divine hiddenness as a widespread experiential and argumentative problem for belief in God.

After O'Connor introduces hiddenness as a form of the problem of evil, Pine grounds universal access in Christian revelation and considers how knowledge of God should permeate personal and social life.
The geographic distribution of religious belief is better explained by human sociology than by a God proactively seeking relationship with everyone.
The argument directly connects uneven religious geography to divine hiddenness and supplies a naturalistic rival explanation for predictable regional differences in belief.
Pine's claim that the Gospel and relationship with Christ are genuinely available to everyone through ordinary human institutions.

O'Connor contrasts heavily Buddhist and heavily theistic populations, rejects innate regional resistance and selective divine concealment as plausible explanations, and favors sociological transmission.
Divine agency should not be modeled as optimization of a best possible world, because creation expresses divine goodness through limited and differentiated creatures.
This rejects a maximizing standard implicitly imposed on God and introduces creaturely differentiation as the framework for explaining unequal conditions and physical evils.
O'Connor's contention that a universally loving God should prevent stark geographic disparities in access to religious belief.
Pine distinguishes divine from creaturely agency, denies that Christianity requires the best possible arrangement, and portrays creation as multiple finite participations in divine goodness.
Even without a best possible world, unequal access to revelation appears unfair when those differences may determine whether people receive eternal life.
The passage refines the hiddenness objection away from global optimization and toward unequal revelatory opportunity, faultlessness, and potentially eternal consequences.
Pine's rejection of a best-possible-world requirement and his account of creation as differentiated expressions of divine goodness.
O'Connor accepts that no maximal world may exist but argues that a relational God's selective provision of experiences still resembles favoritism and demands a defense of divine fairness.
Human equality is not the governing standard of divine justice, because creation is gratuitous and differentiated natural gifts may be complemented by supernatural goods.
This directly contests the fairness premise of the skeptical case and offers gratuitous creation, supernatural compensation, and systemic differentiation as the alternative framework.
O'Connor's argument that unequal revelation is unfair because unchosen access differences can decide a person's eternal fate.
Pine denies a simple symmetry between human and divine justice, treats existence and glory as gifts rather than entitlements, and argues that diverse creatures jointly manifest divine abundance.
A sincere seeker cannot simply choose conviction, so making eternal destiny depend on cognitive limitations or unpersuasive arguments creates a hiddenness-based problem of evil.
This states the sincere-nonbelief route in its strongest form by linking involuntary belief, earnest seeking, limited cognition, and eternal consequences.
Pine's appeal to gratuitous and differentiated divine gifts as an answer to unequal access and the charge of unfairness.
O'Connor describes someone open to worship and moral truth who nevertheless remains unconvinced, then argues that even one sincere nonresistant nonbeliever requires an explanation.
Human freedom is limited but meaningful, and divine revelation may be recognized only across the extended narrative of a life through patient interpretation and perseverance.
The passage answers sincere nonbelief by replacing a momentary evidential test with a temporally extended account of agency, grace, interpretation, and endurance.
O'Connor's claim that sincere seekers cannot choose conviction and may remain faultlessly unconvinced despite earnest investigation.
Pine concedes that human volition is modest, portrays life as many movements rather than one decisive act, and argues that experience and revelation are interpreted more deeply over time.
A lifelong journey cannot secure a hiddenness defense when another person's free action can abruptly end the seeker's opportunity and fix an eternal outcome.
This directly attacks the longitudinal defense by showing how contingent death, other agents' choices, and unequal timing make eternal consequences appear arbitrary.
Pine's proposal that revelation and conversion should be assessed across an entire life requiring patience, interpretation, and perseverance.
O'Connor argues that a future conversion can be prevented by another person's violence, rejects counterfactual salvation as undermining earthly testing, and emphasizes unequal spiritual fortune.
Unequal divine gifts can serve an organic communal good, because differentiated persons function as members of one mystical body rather than as isolated competitors.
This begins a direct account of unequal fortune in which differentiated goods express providential wisdom and benefit a personal, interdependent whole.
O'Connor's charge that unequal opportunities for communion and contingently interrupted seeking make salvation arbitrary and lucky.
Pine invokes divine predilection and the mystical body to argue that unequal goods resemble differentiated organs serving a whole, while beginning to address the objection from severe suffering.
Differences in divine favor do not explain why sincere seekers can remain wholly unable to find a God who supposedly wants relationship with them.
It sharpens the hiddenness challenge into an apparent conflict among divine desire, divine power, sincere seeking, and persistent nonbelief.
Pine's claim that unequal divine gifts belong to a providentially ordered and ultimately personal whole.
After Pine invokes differentiated gifts and an organic providential order, O'Connor distinguishes unequal favor from complete failure of contact despite sincere seeking.
Persistent nonbelief can involve free rejection of an offered sequence of graces, while salvation always originates in grace and damnation in creaturely refusal.
It supplies the principal Catholic agency-based explanation for why universally offered grace need not culminate in belief or salvation.
O'Connor's contention that some sincere seekers appear completely excluded from contact with God despite reaching out.
Pine answers the sincere-seeker problem by distinguishing circumstances outside a person's control from a freely rejectable chain of divine graces.
A person who fully understood eternal suffering and the available supreme good could not rationally reject salvation, so damnation would punish ignorance or impaired reasoning.
It directly attacks the free-rejection defense of hell by arguing that informed refusal is irrational and therefore cannot fairly ground eternal punishment.
Pine's claim that hell results from a person's free rejection of grace rather than from God's withholding of salvation.
After establishing that hell is conscious and eternal, O'Connor argues that rejection must reflect disbelief or defective reasoning rather than culpable informed choice.
Only direct vision of God's essence compels assent; lesser goods and signs remain open to alternative construal, and people bear responsibility for attention, ignorance, weakness, and desire.
It defends the coherence and culpability of rejecting salvation by combining noncompelling evidence with a comparatively strong account of human agency.
O'Connor's argument that anyone rejecting a fully understood offer of salvation must be nonculpably mistaken or irrational.
Pine distinguishes the compelling beatific vision from finite motives and testimony, then treats earthly life as a probationary exercise of responsible agency.
Uneven religious geography is compatible with providence because everyone receives sufficient initial grace, though its historical and cultural mediation can be thinner or thicker.
It provides the principal affirmative account of religious inequality by joining universal sufficient grace to differentiated historical pedagogy and providential care.
O'Connor's broader challenge that unequal access to belief calls for an explanation under a universally loving and relational God.
Pine says natural law and implicit faith begin a grace-led path for every person, while revelation and testimony vary within a wider providential order.
Religious geography makes conversion radically harder for some, whereas the observed cultural variation of religion is more expected if religions are human products.
It converts unequal religious access into a comparative evidential argument contrasting the expectations of universal revelation with those of human cultural production.
Pine's claim that varying forms of testimony remain sufficient and are harmonized by God's universal providential care.
O'Connor emphasizes intellectual and social conversion costs, then compares the globally even access expected from one relational God with observed cultural dependence.
The evidential force of religious geography cannot be inferred from believer counts alone because cultural obstacles, institutional effects, and costly conversions require detailed empirical study.
It resists the skeptical likelihood comparison by disputing the adequacy of its observational measure and reasserting undetermined human volition under pressure.
O'Connor's claim that regional and cultural variation is substantially more expected under a human-origin account of religion.
Pine argues that sociology must assess both barriers and indirect cultural effects, noting that severe social costs do not uniformly determine conversion choices.

If salvation depends on contingent social encounters and trivial choices, outcomes appear arbitrary; if God arranges those encounters, providence threatens freedom and still leaves unequal intervention unexplained.
It presents a dilemma for the agency defense: unplanned contingencies make salvation precarious, while planned contingencies undermine freedom and renew selective-intervention concerns.
Pine's appeal to culturally situated human volition and providential grace as compatible explanations of uneven conversion.
O'Connor traces belief changes to accidental relationships and small decisions, then argues that divine orchestration either compromises free will or remains selectively absent.
Providence offers recurrent opportunities for grace rather than controlling one decisive event, while human resistance and the inherited disorder of original sin explain failures to receive them.
It answers the contingency dilemma by replacing isolated intervention with pervasive grace and locating resistance in wounded but active creaturely agency.
O'Connor's dilemma that contingent conversion is arbitrary unless divinely arranged, in which case freedom and equal intervention become problematic.
Pine portrays grace as continuously available, refusal as a form of obstructing its reception, and present human disorder as inherited loss of original rectitude.

Original sin is the first rational creatures' rejection of their gifted dependence on God, causing loss of grace, integrated powers, immortality, and impassibility without changing human nature itself.
It articulates the original-sin mechanism on which Pine's explanation of disordered agency, culpable resistance, suffering, and the need for restorative grace depends.
After discussion of an evolutionary setting for the first rational humans, Pine describes their initial gifts, their rejection of dependence, and humanity's ensuing deprivation.
The Fall did not fundamentally change human nature but deprived humanity of grace and left intellect, will, and passions less able to order lower goods beneath higher goods.
This explains the Catholic account of what original sin transmits and supplies the causal link between lost grace and present human disorder.
O'Connor's question about what became different in humanity because of the Fall.
After affirming continuity between Adamic and present human nature, Pine explains present disorder as deprivation of grace rather than replacement by another nature.
The Eden account makes inherited suffering morally troubling because the first humans appear already vulnerable, deceived, and possibly without the moral knowledge required for culpability.
The challenge directly attacks whether original sin can fairly explain present suffering when the initiating act itself appears insufficiently voluntary or informed.
Pine's account of the Fall as a culpable rejection whose loss of grace disorders later humanity.
O'Connor argues from the serpent's prior presence, Eve's deception, the tree's association with moral knowledge, and inherited childbirth and labor suffering.

Genesis 1–11 should be read as mythopoeic theological adaptation whose central claims are divine and human goodness, free rejection, loving obedience, and responsibility rather than literal narrative mechanics.
This reframes the disputed Eden details while preserving the doctrinal claims of freedom and responsibility on which Pine's defense of original sin depends.
O'Connor's claim that the literal Eden narrative depicts deception, deficient knowledge, and unjust inherited punishment.
Pine locates Genesis among adapted ancient Near Eastern stories and treats angelic, individual, and communal responsibility as the account's theological core.

Treating present deprivation as a consequence of an ancestor's deceived act remains analogous to a landlord tormenting a tenant for a great-grandfather's breach and therefore entails intolerable inherited guilt.
The analogy isolates the alleged injustice of transferring deprivation or blame across generations and presses the main moral objection to original sin.
Pine's appeal to free rejection and shared individual, communal, and angelic responsibility for the Fall.
O'Connor imagines a landlord imposing severe living conditions because an ancestor was deceived into breaching a poorly explained condition.
The better analogy is not imposed torment but humanity's refusal of an unmerited palace: original grace exceeded what justice required, and humanity chose the condition of nature left to itself.
The revised analogy denies that fallen existence is an externally imposed punishment and instead construes it as withdrawal of a gratuitous supernatural gift.
O'Connor's landlord analogy alleging inherited punishment and inherited moral blame.
Pine contrasts an abusive landlord with creatures questioning God's intentions, refusing gratuitous palace-like grace, and receiving the natural condition they selected.
Present people did not choose Adam's refusal, and even granting some virtual presence in his decision cannot establish culpability when Adam and Eve acted through deception.
This directly contests both components of Pine's defense: collective participation in Adam and the claim that the originating choice was sufficiently culpable.
Pine's claim that humanity collectively chose against gratuitous grace and was consequently left to itself.
O'Connor denies remembering or endorsing the ancestral choice, says he would prefer grace, and reiterates that the serpent's deception undermines culpability.

A literalistic reading distorts Genesis; its compositional and traditional setting communicates God's goodness, humanity's goodness, culpable choice, and responsibility more reliably than its surface narrative details.
The interpretive distinction protects the doctrinal argument from objections dependent on treating the serpent, fruit, and chronology as straightforward historical description.
O'Connor's renewed contention that the surface story portrays Adam and Eve as deceived rather than culpable.
Pine distinguishes the text's literal theological sense from literalism and appeals to authorship, redaction, tradition, and comparison with ancient Near Eastern myths.

Original sin is inherited as human nature deprived of superadded grace, not as an added guilty defect, while Adam represents humanity as its origin and best-equipped member and restoration remains personally available in salvation.
This supplies the substantive Catholic mechanism for solidarity in Adam while denying inherited personal blame and connecting lost gifts to baptism, virtue, and resurrection.
O'Connor's objections that nobody now chose Adam's act and that deception defeats both ancestral and inherited culpability.
Pine describes presence in Adam through shared nature, descent, and representative excellence, then presents grace and the lost gifts as recoverable within salvation history.
Even if one imagines oneself in Adam's position, deception by a uniquely intelligent evil agent would not justify condemning the deceived person, much less that person's descendants.
The move argues that Pine's strongest account of human representation still fails because the initiating act lacks the culpability required to ground its consequences.
Pine's claim that Adam represented humanity as its best-equipped member and that people likely would have made the same choice.
O'Connor compares Eden to being tricked into unknowingly uttering blasphemy and argues that neither the speaker nor later generations could fairly be condemned.
O'Connor's sustained theological study, worship attendance, attempted prayer, and openness to others' prayers constitute extensive seeking, yet he reports receiving no discernible divine response.
This provides a concrete case of apparently sincere and persistent nonbelief, directly bearing on whether divine hiddenness counts against Catholic theism.
Pine's request for an account of how O'Connor has sought God without finding and whether his conception of God has developed.
O'Connor acknowledges uncertain motives but recounts a theology degree, changed views, church attendance, biblical study, attempted prayer, and respectful religious participation.
Cultural conditioning and fallibility need not invalidate religious commitment, because reflective inquiry can remain an organic and continuing feature of a situated life.
The account directly engages the role of cultural and ethnic formation in belief while conceding fallibility and defending continued inquiry from within a religious commitment.
O'Connor's concern that prolonged inquiry may still be fundamentally misguided and that cultural formation makes the correctness of one's approach difficult to ascertain.

Pine recounts being challenged over the cultural limitations of his theological proposals, acknowledges his own conditioning and arrogance, and presents questioning as an enduring feature of his religious life.

Persistent questioning may progressively enlarge a person's capacity to recognize and receive an answer, even when divine response initially takes the form of deeper questions rather than a direct solution.
This supplies a direct theistic explanation for apparent divine silence: inquiry and delayed disclosure can form the subject's capacity for an answer rather than indicate divine absence.
O'Connor's claim that sustained sincere searching has produced no discernible response from God and therefore gives him reason to regard divine hiddenness as a serious problem.
Using Job as a model, Pine argues that people seek immediate solutions but may instead receive partial indications and formative questions that prepare them for fuller understanding over time.
The Book of Job appears to portray God as inflicting suffering for a wager and then rebuking the sufferer for seeking an explanation, which conflicts with divine love and compassion.

The objection challenges Pine's formative reading of unanswered suffering by arguing that the scriptural model instead depicts morally troubling divine conduct incompatible with Catholic claims about God's character.
Pine's appeal to the Book of Job as showing that divine counterquestions deepen inquiry and progressively prepare human beings to recognize and receive an eventual solution.

O'Connor grants that a metaphorical reading might be more complex but argues that the narrative's apparent refusal of explanation is harsh rather than compassionate and leaves the story morally troubling.

Read canonically through the New Testament, divine questioning can provoke the very insight needed for revelation, while suffering may create capacities through which a larger providential story becomes visible.

This is Pine's final defense of the formative account of hiddenness and suffering, connecting divine questions, progressive receptivity, revelation, and providential meaning while acknowledging suffering's destructive reality.
O'Connor's objection that God's response to Job is contemptuous, withholds a deserved explanation, and appears inconsistent with the loving and compassionate nature attributed to God.

Pine interprets scriptural dialogue through Christ's question-driven revelations, argues that people must become capable of receiving divine glory, and cautiously situates suffering within a potentially larger story.
